content: A joint is the anatomical location where two or more bones come into contact. Joints are designed to facilitate movement and provide mechanical support to the body. They are classified based on their structural and functional characteristics. Classification of Joints Joints are primarily classified in two ways: structurally and functionally. Structural classification is determined by the way bones are connected to one another, while functional classification is based on the degree of movement permitted between the articulating bones. In practice, there is often significant overlap between these two classification systems. For example, highly mobile diarthroses are always synovial joints. While diarthroses refers to the functional classification, synovial joints refers to the structural classification. These terms are often used interchangeably. Singular terms for joints end in -sis, while their plural forms end in -ses. Structural Classification Structural classification categorizes joints based on how the bones are connected. There are three main types of structural classifications: 1. Fibrous Joints (Immovable Joints): These joints are connected by dense connective tissue, primarily composed of collagen. Fibrous joints are further divided into three subtypes: Sutures: Found between the bones of the skull. In fetal skulls, sutures are wide to allow slight movement during birth. These sutures later become rigid and immovable (synarthrodial). Syndesmoses: Found between long bones, such as the radius and ulna in the forearm or the tibia and fibula in the leg. Unlike other fibrous joints, syndesmoses are slightly movable (amphiarthrodial), though not as mobile as synovial joints. Gomphoses: These are specialized joints between the root of a tooth and its socket in the maxilla or mandible. 2. Cartilaginous Joints: These joints are entirely connected by cartilage and allow more movement than fibrous joints but less than synovial joints. Examples include the joint between the manubrium and the sternum. Cartilaginous joints also form the growth regions of immature long bones and the intervertebral discs of the spinal column. Primary Cartilaginous Joints (Synchondroses): Bones are connected by hyaline cartilage or fibrocartilage, sometimes occurring between ossification centers. This cartilage may ossify with age. Examples include the joint between the first rib and the manubrium of the sternum, as well as growth plates in long bones. These joints typically allow no movement or minimal movement, as seen in the manubriosternal and first manubriocostal joints. Secondary Cartilaginous Joints (Symphyses): These are fibrocartilaginous joints, usually located in the midline of the body. Examples include the intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis. These joints allow limited movement. 3. Synovial Joints: Synovial joints have a space between the articulating bones filled with synovial fluid. These joints are the most mobile of all joint types and include the knee and shoulder. Synovial joints are further classified into six subtypes based on their structure and movement: Ball and Socket Joints: Found in the shoulder and hip. Hinge Joints: Found in the elbow. Pivot Joints: Found between the radius and ulna. Condyloid (Ellipsoidal) Joints: Found in the wrist (between the radius and carpals) and the knee. Saddle Joints: Found in the joint between the carpal bone of the thumb and the metacarpal. Gliding Joints: Found between the carpal bones. Functional Classification Joints can also be classified based on their functional properties, specifically the degree of mobility they allow: 1. Synarthrosis (Immovable Joints): These joints permit little or no movement. Most synarthroses are fibrous joints. They can be further categorized based on how the bones are joined: Synchondroses: Joints where two bones are connected by cartilage. Synostoses: Joints where two initially separate bones eventually fuse into one. For example, the plates of the cranium fuse together as a child matures into adulthood. Premature fusion of cranial plates can lead to deformities and brain damage due to restricted skull expansion, a condition known as craniosynostosis. 2. Amphiarthrosis (Slightly Movable Joints): These joints allow slight movement. The articulating bone surfaces are covered in hyaline cartilage and joined by strands of fibrocartilage. Most amphiarthroses are cartilaginous joints. 3. Diarthrosis (Freely Movable Joints): These joints allow a wide range of movements (e.g., flexion, adduction, pronation) and are exclusively synovial joints. Diarthroses are divided into six classes based on their structure and movement: Ball and Socket Joints: Such as the shoulder or hip. Hinge Joints: Such as the elbow. Pivot Joints: Such as the radius and ulna. Condyloid Joints: Such as the wrist or knee. Saddle Joints: Such as the thumb joint. Gliding Joints: Such as those between the carpal bones. Biomechanical Classification Joints can also be classified based on their anatomy or biomechanical properties. According to anatomical classification, joints are subdivided into simple and compound joints based on the number of bones involved, as well as into complex and combination joints. Simple Joints: Involve two articulating surfaces (e.g., shoulder joint, hip joint). Compound Joints: Involve three or more articulating surfaces.
